name: The Assumption Lab
description: Revisit the fundamentals through liquidity, opportunity cost, compounding, and uncertainty.
tone: The model is confident. Ask it why.

topics.title: Separate flows, stocks, and constraints.
topics.text: Before admiring the balance sheet, ask what can pay a bill on Tuesday. Income and spending are flows over time. Net worth is a stock: assets minus liabilities at a point in time. Liquidity asks how readily resources can meet a cash demand without unacceptable cost or delay. Start with obligations, deadlines, and uncertainty, then consider the return. Tuesday rarely accepts a promising long-term projection.
topics.aside: This fictional household has $6,000 of monthly take-home cash and $4,200 of essential outflows. We have left net worth and job stability unspecified. Useful missing facts deserve to be noticed.
topics.joke: Your house has equity. The grocery checkout prefers something more portable.
topics.prompt: Inspect the cash flow. Notice what the illustration cannot tell you.
topics.term: A STRONG BALANCE SHEET CAN STILL HAVE A TIMING PROBLEM
topics.everyday: A household can have substantial home equity and a very awkward gap between bills and self-employment receipts. A smaller balance sheet may support a steadier plan when cash and liabilities line up. Separate spendable income from paper gains, restricted assets, and fresh borrowing. Account for deductions, too. Then identify which bills are certain, which resources are conditional, and which dates will refuse to move. Those distinctions earn their space in the model.
topics.connection: Name the cash flow, wealth, and binding constraint before asking the model to find an optimum.
words: An amount measured over time, such as a month’s income.
An amount at a particular time, such as today’s net worth.
The ability to meet a cash demand without an unacceptable wait or cost.
Something that limits the choices the plan can actually make.
topics.assumptions: All money amounts and timing are invented for teaching. This is not a survey of prices, income, or tax rates. The flow view is a single example, not a recommended allocation.

topics.title: Allocate marginal dollars deliberately.
topics.text: Ask each extra dollar what its next-best job would be. That alternative is its opportunity cost. A budget helps compare uses of money within real constraints: fixed costs, taxes, care obligations, and income uncertainty. Before calling a surplus investable, check which upcoming liabilities have been left off the guest list. An annual bill remains real even when the monthly spreadsheet has forgotten its name.
topics.aside: The modeled essentials leave $1,800. Adjust flexible spending and watch the time to a $12,000 goal. Growth, income volatility, and additional taxes are outside this small experiment.
topics.joke: “All else equal” has once again failed to attend the meeting.
topics.prompt: Explore the allocation, then ask which missing fact would matter.
topics.term: OPTIMIZE WITHIN CONSTRAINTS; AUDIT THE CONSTRAINTS
topics.everyday: A useful spending plan has to work, withstand some trouble, and support the goals the household actually has. Compare the next dollar’s possible uses and distinguish commitments from choices you can reverse. Percentage rules need context. Stress a plan that assumes uninterrupted income, one price path, or endlessly flexible due dates. Then reconcile the surplus with irregular bills. Elegant allocation is more useful after the missing obligations have been invited back in.
topics.connection: Spending, debt repayment, reserves, and investing are all possible jobs for a dollar. Opportunity cost helps you compare them.
words: Deciding what to do with the next available dollar or unit of resources.
The next-best alternative you give up by choosing.
Whether the plan can work within the constraints it actually faces.
An obligation that arrives less neatly than a regular monthly bill.
topics.assumptions: Essentials are fixed in this illustration. Flexible spending and saving divide the remaining money. Goal periods = ceiling(goal ÷ saving per period). No interest, price changes, or income changes are modeled.

topics.title: Liquidity is an option with a cost.
topics.text: Accessible cash can look unambitious until it prevents a forced loan or asset sale. Holding it has an opportunity cost, but having it available can matter greatly in a shock. Insurance transfers specified losses, with deductibles, exclusions, and questions about coverage and payment. Look across income, assets, obligations, and available support. The household needs a plan that can function when several things become inconvenient at once.
topics.aside: Begin with $1,000, add a monthly contribution for six months, and test a $2,500 shock. The scenario has no assigned probability and includes no insurance recovery.
topics.joke: An illiquid asset is excellent at saying, “I’m worth a lot, technically.”
topics.prompt: Change contributions. Observe the uncovered cost, not just the balance.
topics.term: STRESS A PLAN AGAINST AN OBLIGATION
topics.everyday: Cash reserves may earn less than a risky alternative while still helping the overall plan. They preserve options during job loss or a market decline, especially when income and asset values weaken together. Read insurance as a contract for specified coverage. Check limits, exclusions, deductibles, the provider’s ability to pay, and reimbursement timing before counting an insurance payment as cash on hand. “Covered eventually” and “payable today” can be an awkward distance apart.
topics.connection: Test whether the bill can be paid under stress, as well as whether average wealth increases. Both questions deserve an answer.
words: The usefulness of having money ready when a cash need appears.
Risks that can get worse together, just when you would prefer some variety.
An agreement that shifts specified losses, such as insurance coverage.
Trying a defined adverse scenario to see whether the plan still works.
topics.assumptions: Savings = starting cash + contribution × periods. A surprise is subtracted once when switched on. Savings cannot go below zero; the remaining cost is shown separately. No interest, investment returns, insurance payment, or new borrowing is included.

topics.title: Debt repayment changes the opportunity set.
topics.text: Debt repayment can avoid contractual interest; a risky investment offers a less certain result. That is a useful starting comparison, with liquidity, taxes, penalties, and flexibility still at the table. APR may not include every relevant product cost. Use the actual terms, and ask what happens if income falls. An expected return can wait while you check whether the payment schedule survives contact with real life.
topics.aside: Try fixed payments on $10,000 at 9% APR. Each month, the model charges the opening balance × APR ÷ 12, then applies the payment. Taxes, fees, and new borrowing are excluded.
topics.joke: The expected return has a beautiful résumé. The debt payment has a due date.
topics.prompt: Compare payment speeds without treating this model as a recommendation.
topics.everyday: A stated borrowing rate and a probability-weighted investment return need careful comparison. Deductibility, prepayment terms, rate resets, and accessible cash can all affect the decision. This model leaves those features aside so you can inspect repayment arithmetic. If a payment cannot cover interest, the starting balance does not decline. For products with daily interest or changing rates, bring the actual contract and payment dates back into the calculation.
topics.connection: Put debt costs, liquidity, and investment risk on a consistent after-cost footing before asking which choice looks best.
words: Paying down a debt through scheduled payments.
An annualized percentage measure of borrowing cost; check the conventions for the product.
When unpaid interest can be added to the balance, leaving more debt to repay.
topics.assumptions: Interest = opening balance × APR ÷ 12, then the fixed payment is applied. The last payment may be smaller. No new charges, fees, daily calculation, payment timing variation, or tax effects. The comparison payment is a fictional fixed amount, not a real issuer’s minimum-payment schedule.

topics.title: Audit nominal growth, fees, and inflation.
topics.text: Compounding is patient, and ongoing costs are happy to be patient with it. Nominal values count account dollars. Inflation-adjusted values ask what those dollars can buy. Diversification can reduce concentration risk while leaving market risk. Keep asking what the smooth curve leaves out: a single expected path cannot show the full range of outcomes or promise that a future bill will be covered.
topics.aside: Compare your selected annual fee with a fictional 0.1% fee under the same assumptions. Returns, fees, and inflation stay constant here. All values are before tax.
topics.joke: Decimals: tiny on the fee sheet, surprisingly ambitious over twenty years.
topics.prompt: Move fees and inflation. Then stress the ending value with a 20% fall.
topics.term: THE OUTPUT IS ONLY AS USEFUL AS THE ASSUMPTIONS
topics.everyday: Hold gross return constant and a higher ongoing fee leaves less money compounding. Adjust for inflation to translate the balance into buying power; taxes need another layer. Now consider an invented one-period investment: an 80% chance of gaining 15% and a 20% chance of losing 40%. Its expected return is 4%, but the 20% chance of that 40% loss has not politely disappeared. Averages are useful. They do not pay a bill on your behalf.
topics.connection: Ask what decision the model helps you make, what downside it reveals, and which assumptions need another look.
words: The balance in account dollars, before adjusting for inflation.
What the money can buy at the relevant price level.
The average return when each possible outcome is weighted by its modeled probability.
Changing assumptions to see which ones move the answer.
topics.assumptions: Nominal ending value = principal × (1 + (gross return − annual fee)/100)^years. Purchasing power divides that value by (1 + inflation/100)^years. Subtracting the fee from annual return is a simplified convention. The optional 20% drop is applied once at the end, to both comparison paths. No taxes, contributions, or changing returns. These are scenarios, not promised outcomes.

recap: Separate cash flow, net worth, and liquidity.
Evaluate resilience before chasing an optimum.
Compare fees, purchasing power, and downside risk.
action: Name an assumption that could reverse a decision.
Check a plan against a shorter deadline.
Compare costs using actual product terms.
artAlt: An analysis screen with two growth paths and a magnifying glass questioning the assumptions.

review.title: The assumption audit
review.intro: Five claims enter the lab. Bring your skepticism; the spreadsheet has already brought its confidence.
summary: Solvency across a period does not guarantee liquidity on every due date.
Opportunity cost connects an allocation to the alternatives it displaces.
Liquidity reserves and risk transfer address different exposures; assumptions determine the gaps.
Amortization depends on rate, payment, and timing. Payments must exceed interest to reduce principal in this model.
Separate nominal value from purchasing power, account for fees, and test adverse scenarios. A deterministic path is not a forecast.

questions.prompt: What can a positive month-end balance fail to establish?
choices: Whether any money arrived during the month
Whether every obligation could be met on its due date
questions.explanation: An aggregate surplus does not establish liquidity at each point in time. A dated cash-flow path can reveal an interim funding gap. The sum is correct; its alibi is incomplete.

questions.prompt: What does opportunity cost add to an allocation decision?
choices: The value of the alternative forgone
A guarantee of the selected outcome
A rule to maximize only current consumption
questions.explanation: An allocation uses resources that could serve another goal. Evaluating the displaced alternative makes the choice explicit; it does not prescribe the same priorities for everyone.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish liquid reserves from insurance coverage?
choices: A reserve guarantees every loss can be funded
They address different exposures and can leave different gaps
questions.explanation: Insurance transfers specified risks under terms that may include deductibles and exclusions. Liquidity supports cash needs, including timing gaps. Neither label alone establishes full resilience.

questions.prompt: In the monthly debt model, a payment equals that month’s interest. What happens to principal?
choices: It falls by the full payment
questions.explanation: The payment covers interest but leaves nothing to reduce principal. Under these assumptions, paying off the balance requires more than the accrued interest. The principal has renewed its lease.

questions.prompt: What does an inflation-adjusted ending value represent?
choices: Ending account dollars expressed in today’s buying power
A tax-adjusted return in all circumstances
questions.explanation: Dividing nominal value by the modeled inflation factor estimates purchasing power in today’s dollars. Fees, taxes, and uncertainty remain separate considerations; this illustration does not model taxes.
